meta.descriptionEn: In November 1992, a farmer lost a hammer in a Suffolk field and asked a friend with a metal detector to help find it. What the detector found instead was something no one expected: silver spoons, gold jewellery and coin after coin. It would become the largest hoard of late Roman gold and silver ever found in Britain, with 14,865 coins and about 200 precious objects. But who buried it, and why? Was it fear of invasion, a gift-exchange system that collapsed, or even the proceeds of a robbery? Follow the dramatic excavation, the press frenzy, the valuation, the hidden clues in the spoons and jewellery, and the story of how one lucky find changed the law in England.
meta.descriptionUr: November 1992 mein Suffolk ke ek khet mein ek kisan ka hathora kho gaya. Dost ne metal detector se talash shuru ki, magar nikla kuch aur hi: chaandi ke chamche, sone ke zewar aur sikkon ka khazana. Ye Britain mein mila sab se bara late Roman sone chaandi ka zakhira tha. Magar isay kis ne dafnaya, aur kyun? Kya hamle ka dar tha, ya koi chori ka maal? Is documentary mein dekhein khudai, khazane ke raaz, aur kaise is ek dariyaft ne England ka qanoon badal diya.

articleEn: On 16 November 1992, in the village of Hoxne in Suffolk, England, an ordinary day unfolded in an ordinary field. A farmer named Peter Whatling had lost his hammer, and he asked his friend Eric Lawes for help. Lawes was a retired gardener and keen amateur metal detectorist. He began sweeping his detector over the field.

Instead of a hammer, the ground gave up something very different: a treasure from history. The detector sounded, and after only a few items were lifted out, silver spoons, gold jewellery and a great many gold and silver coins came into view.

Then Lawes made a very wise decision. The two men dug no further and informed the landowners, Suffolk County Council, and the police. This one decision is what makes the story so special. Had everything been pulled out in a hurry, the original arrangement of the hoard might have been lost forever.

So how big was this treasure? Who buried it? And most important, why was it buried? This article looks at how the whole hoard was recovered in a single day, the uproar in the newspapers, and the valuable objects inside. The story begins with a lost hammer, but it ends with a law that changed how treasure is handled in England.

articleEn: To understand the hoard, we have to go back in time. Roman Britain lasted from 43 AD to 410 AD, roughly 367 years. In 43 AD, on the orders of Claudius, four legions invaded, and the Romans made Britain a province called Britannia. In the early fourth century it was divided into four provinces, overseen by a vicarius who answered to the praetorian prefect based at Trier.

The peace did not last. In 367 the Saxons, Picts, Scoti and Attacotti attacked together in what is called the Great Conspiracy, and it shook Roman Britain badly. From 368, Theodosius the Elder carried out military and civil reforms and created a new province named Valentia. In 383, Magnus Maximus declared himself emperor at Segontium in north Wales and crossed the English Channel. His campaigns needed soldiers from Britain, so some forts, such as Chester, may have been emptied. His time ended in 388. Around 396 new attacks came, and Stilicho led a punitive expedition. Peace is said to have been restored by 399. But by 401 more troops had been called away to help in the war against Alaric I.

Coins were becoming scarcer in this period. Coins from 378 to 388 are very rare, and after 402 even copper coins are found only rarely. In 406 the Suebi, Alans and Vandals crossed the frozen Rhine and swept into Gaul, leaving the western provinces exposed. The remaining Roman soldiers in Britain feared that invaders would cross the Channel, so they chose emperors of their own. The first two were killed by the army within months. The third was a soldier, Constantine III, who was chosen as emperor in 407. He took an army to Gaul and won some successes, but Honorius's forces defeated him, and his story ended in 411. His departure left Britain weaker against Saxon and Irish raiders.

Zosimus writes that in 409 the locals expelled the Roman civilian administration. Here there is disagreement. Some believe Zosimus was really describing the Bagaudae revolt in Armorica, not Britain. Then, in 410, a letter came from Honorius, traditionally read as a refusal of Britain's appeal for help, though it may have been addressed to Bruttium or Bologna. Saint Jerome afterwards called Britain a 'province fertile of tyrants'. This hints that central authority had weakened and local strongmen were rising.
And it was in this crumbling world, sometime after 408, that someone was burying an oak chest in a Suffolk field.

articleEn: On 17 November 1992, the day after the discovery, a team from the Suffolk Archaeological Unit arrived at the site for an emergency excavation. The field lay south-west of Hoxne village. The land belonged to Suffolk County Council, and Peter Whatling worked it as a tenant farmer.

The most surprising fact is that the whole hoard was excavated in a single day. It held 14,865 coins and about 200 other items. Rather than separating pieces on site, the team lifted several large blocks weighing many tons so they could be opened up in the laboratory. The search was then widened. Within a 30-metre radius of the find spot, the ground was scanned with metal detectors to make sure nothing else had been left behind. And the lost hammer? It was found too. Peter Whatling's hammer was later donated to the British Museum. Consider this: the search for a hammer brought to light the largest hoard of late Roman silver and gold ever found in Britain.

The most important thing in the dig was not the coins or jewels themselves but the way they had been placed in the ground. The hoard lay in one spot, inside the completely decayed remains of a wooden chest. The wood had nearly vanished, but pieces of fittings such as hinges and locks were recovered. Inside, objects had not been thrown in at random. Ladles and bowls had been stacked inside one another, and the rest were grouped as if they had been kept in an internal box. This let archaeologists understand the original layout.

Some items had been slightly damaged by burrowing animals and ploughing, but overall disturbance was very small. The main reason was Eric Lawes's prompt report, which let professional archaeologists excavate the hoard in situ, in its original position. Had Lawes kept removing everything himself, the existence of the chest and the order inside it might never have been known.

Hoards are often taken out in haste or have already been scattered by farming, so details of organic materials are rarely found. At Hoxne, organic traces survived: wheat straw, fine marks of linen, and fragments of nine kinds of wood. The hoard had been lifted in a day, but the story was not over. It was taken to the British Museum for cleaning and conservation.

articleEn: By the time the hoard reached the British Museum, word had already got out. The discovery had leaked to the press, and everyone was about to start talking about it. On 19 November the newspaper The Sun printed a story on its front page, with a photo of Eric Lawes holding his metal detector. The paper claimed the treasure was worth £10 million, though at that point nobody knew the full contents or value of the hoard.

In response to this unexpected publicity, the British Museum held a press conference on 20 November and formally announced the discovery. Then something interesting happened: the newspapers lost interest very quickly. That was good news for the curators, who could now sort, clean and stabilise the hoard without interruption. Initial cleaning and basic conservation were finished within a month of the discovery.

But the real question remained: who legally owned the treasure? That had to be decided in a coroner's court. On 3 September 1993 a coroner's inquest was held at Lowestoft, and the hoard was declared treasure trove. Treasure trove meant it had been hidden with the intention of recovering it later. Under English common law, such an object becomes the property of the Crown if no owner comes forward.

The custom at the time, however, was that a person who found treasure trove and reported it at once would receive a reward equal to its market value. The sum was paid by the national institution that wished to acquire the treasure. In other words, the reward matched what the hoard was worth.

In November 1993 the Treasure Trove Reviewing Committee set the value of the hoard at £1.75 million, which is about £3.77 million in 2025 terms. The whole sum was paid to Eric Lawes as the finder, and he shared it with the farmer, Peter Whatling. Later, the Treasure Act of 1996 allowed the finder, the tenant and the landowner all to share in the reward, a point we return to at the end.
So the price was settled. But what exactly lay behind that £1.75 million? In the next part we open the chest.

articleEn: So what was inside the chest? Counting everything, the hoard held 14,865 Roman gold, silver and bronze coins. Besides these there were about 200 other objects, including silver tableware and gold jewellery.

Here is the breakdown. There were 569 gold coins called solidi. There were 14,272 silver coins, made up of 60 miliarenses and 14,212 siliquae. There were also 24 bronze nummi. The jewellery came to 29 gold items, and there were 98 silver spoons and ladles. In total this comes to roughly 3.5 kg of gold and 23.75 kg of silver. All of it was packed in an oak chest measuring about 60 x 45 x 30 cm. Some items were in small boxes of yew and cherry wood, while others were wrapped in woollen cloth or hay.

Take the gold coins first. Each solidus weighs about 4.48 grams and was 99% gold. Together the solidi weigh about 8 Roman pounds. Some experts think the coins were separated by weighing rather than by counting. The silver siliquae had a purity between 95% and 99%. Among them, 428 were locally made imitations, usually of good quality. A few coins were forgeries, with silver foil wrapped around a base-metal core, but these are very rare.

Another odd detail is that almost every siliqua had its edge cut off, a practice called clipping. Outside Britain, clipped coins are very rare in the Roman Empire. Why the clipping happened is still debated. Possible explanations include fraud, an attempt to keep the gold-to-silver ratio stable, or a new source of silver bullion.

Coins are the objects whose date and place can be known with certainty. Many carry the emperor's name. The coins come from 14 different mints, including Trier, Arles, Lyon, Rome, Milan, Constantinople and Antioch. The gold coins run from the reign of Valentinian I to Honorius. The silver coins are older still, going back to the time of Constantine II. The very latest coins are of Honorius and Constantine III. Because these belong to their early period, the earliest possible date for the hoard is 408. This matches the life of the Eastern emperor Arcadius, who died in 408, though some sources give a date after 407.

In Roman Britain, only the Eye Hoard held more gold coins. It was found in 1780 or 1781, and its record is rather weak. So those were the coins. But the real surprise was still to come, because the chest also held objects that astonish people even today.

articleEn: Now we come to the most beautiful part of the hoard. First is the gold body chain, considered the most important gold item. It has four fine braided gold chains made in a loop-in-loop style, joined to plaques at the front and back. The front plaque has a large amethyst surrounded by four small garnets. Between them are four empty settings that may once have held pearls. At the centre of the back section is a solidus of Gratian. It may have been an old family keepsake.

In all, the jewellery included one body chain, six necklaces, three rings and 19 bracelets. Together they weigh about 1 kg, with gold purity of about 91.5%. One bracelet carries a Latin inscription: VTERE FELIX DOMINA IVLIANE, meaning 'Lady Juliane, use this happily'. It is the only inscribed gold item in the whole hoard. There are also three sets of four bracelets each. Such sets are very unusual, and they may have been worn two at a time on each arm.

Now to the silver. There are four pepper pots, called piperatoria in Latin. The most famous is the 'Empress' pepper pot, in the form of a wealthy or imperial woman. Her hair, jewellery and clothes are finely made, and she holds a scroll in her left hand. The other three are shaped as Hercules and Antaeus, an ibex, and a hare and hound. Each has a mechanism in its base that turns an inner disc, opening or closing two holes. When the holes were half open, spice could be sprinkled on food. It was probably black pepper, an expensive spice. A tablet from Vindolanda records a quantity of pepper bought for two denarii, so pepper really was sold in Roman Britain.

The silver tigress is a solid cast figure weighing 480 grams and measuring 15.9 cm long. It was made as the handle of a vessel. Under its belly are six clear teats, so it is female. The stripes are made of two engraved lines with black niello between them. But the long body and the arrangement of the stripes do not match a real tiger exactly. The long line along the back looks like that of a tabby cat.

Some small toiletry items were found too. Some are picks and others perhaps scrapers, sized for cleaning teeth or applying cosmetics. X-ray fluorescence analysis showed that the silver items have an average purity of 96%, and the gilded objects carry traces of mercury, meaning mercury gilding was used. A gold armlet showed traces of hematite, probably used for polishing by a jeweller. This is the earliest documented use of the technique in Roman jewellery.

articleEn: Many objects in the Hoxne Hoard carry names in Latin. In all, eight different people are named, seven on spoons and one on a single beaker. The names are Aurelius Ursicinus, Datianus, Euherius, Faustinus, Peregrinus, Quintus, Sanctus and Silvicola. The name appearing most often is Aurelius Ursicinus. There is no historical record of an Aurelius Ursicinus in Britain in this period. There was a Marcus Aurelius Ursicinus in Rome's Praetorian Guard between 222 and 235. Tomlin suggests that the name Aurelius sounds old-fashioned. It suits a provincial landowner better than a military officer or official.

Another name was Faustinus. Soon after the discovery, some people wondered whether it came from Villa Faustini, listed in the Antonine Itinerary. The exact location of Villa Faustini is unknown. Because it was the first station after Colchester, it was thought to lie on the Pye Road, perhaps near Scole. Scole is about 3.2 km north-west of Hoxne, and had a Roman settlement from the first to the fourth century. But this theory was later rejected. The reason was simple: Faustinus was a common name at the time, and it appears on only one spoon. Deciding the owner of the whole hoard from a name on one object is seen as a weak argument.

So where are other clues? Several spoons carry the Chi-Rho symbol, sometimes with alpha and omega. One spoon has vivas in deo written on it, and a necklace clasp also has a Chi-Rho. No clear pagan inscription was found. For this reason some experts believe the goods may have belonged to a Christian household, or perhaps several households.

Now consider what is missing. The hoard has no brooches, pendants or earrings, and no jewellery set with gems, although these were fashionable then. Large silver serving vessels, like those in the Mildenhall Treasure, are also missing. Catherine Johns suggests that the owner's favourite everyday jewellery may never have been buried. In other words, the hoard may have been only part of the owner's wealth. Land, livestock and buildings were separate. It could be a small part of a rich family's fortune.

Another question concerns the nearby Eye Hoard. In 1781, workers at Clint Farm found about 600 Roman gold coins in a lead box, but they were scattered. Another theory is that of a military family. Most coins date between 394 and 405, so some people made this guess. According to it, the family would have come to Britain with Count Theodosius in 368-369, and perhaps left with Constantine III in 407. This is only speculation.

articleEn: Now the biggest question: why was the treasure buried? Nobody knows, and perhaps nobody ever will. But there are some clues. The first is that the hoard was buried with great care, at a distance from any building. The objects were arranged by type in the oak chest. Then came the 1994 excavation, in which the Suffolk County Council Archaeological Service re-excavated the burial site and found a single post hole in the south-west corner. It may have been the position of a marker post, so that those who buried the hoard could find it easily later. That is a guess, not proof.

In the same excavation, soil was removed in 10 cm layers and metal detectors were run over an area of 1,000 square metres. They found 335 Roman items, mostly coins. But no Roman-period building was found, meaning there was no Roman building in the immediate vicinity. The hoard was hidden away from buildings.

The coins tell an interesting story too. In 1994 coins were found scattered around the hoard site in an ellipse running east-west, up to 20 metres on each side. The cause was ploughing. The farmer had ploughed deeply east-west in 1990, whereas before that, from 1967 or 1968, ploughing had run north-south. And in a September 1993 survey, after ploughing, four gold coins and 81 silver coins were found. All were considered part of this same hoard.

Now the three theories put forward by scholars. The first is that someone deliberately hid the wealth to keep it safe, perhaps in the chaos of fifth-century Britain. Roman authority was weakening, much of the army had gone, and Saxon attacks were beginning. This is one possible reason. The second theory is Peter Guest's. According to him, these objects were used in a system of gift exchange. When Britain separated from the Roman Empire, there was no longer a need for them. The third theory is completely different: that this was the loot from a robbery, buried to avoid being caught. Which theory is right? Nobody knows.

Now a comparison. Many hoards from roughly 350 to 450 have been found, mostly on the edges of the Empire. Mildenhall had large dishes, while Hoxne does not. The Thetford and Beaurains hoards contained mostly coins, jewellery and small tableware, and these are perhaps regarded as pagan votive offerings. In the Traprain Law hoard in Scotland, Roman silver had been cut up and bent. That suggests only the value of the metal mattered, perhaps loot from a raid.

articleEn: Now the next stage of the story. In April 1994 the British Museum bought the hoard. But the museum's whole purchase fund at that time was only 1.4 million pounds, while 1.75 million pounds was needed. To make up the difference, donors such as the National Heritage Memorial Fund, the National Art Collections Fund and the J. Paul Getty Trust stepped forward. The value is interesting to work out: the 1993 valuation of 1.75 million pounds comes to about 3.77 million pounds in 2025 terms.

Display began soon. Some items were put on show in the museum in September 1993, and from 1994 to 1995 a large part was shown at Ipswich Museum. Since 1997 the most important pieces have been on permanent display in the Roman Britain gallery in London, Room 49, alongside the Thetford Hoard and close to the Mildenhall Treasure. In 2003 a touring exhibition called Treasure: Finding Our Past visited five cities. A perspex reconstruction of the chest was made for it, and it is now kept in London.

Research followed. Peter Guest published the first full catalogue of the coins in 2005, and Catherine Johns published the catalogue of the remaining objects in 2010. In the 2003 BBC Television documentary Our Top Ten Treasures, the hoard was ranked third among Britain's archaeological finds. And in the 2010 BBC Radio 4 series A History of the World in 100 Objects, the Empress pepper pot was chosen as item 40.

But the biggest effect of the discovery was on the law. Eric Lawes reported the find at once, so archaeologists were able to carry out a fully professional excavation. This improved relations between archaeologists and metal detectorists. Archaeologists were pleased, and detectorists noted that Lawes's effort was praised. The old system was the common-law treasure trove. Then came the Treasure Act 1996, under which the finder, tenant and landowner can share in the reward. The Hoxne discovery and its publicity were one reason for this change. The new law also takes account of technology such as metal detectors. It encourages finders to report, and it also considers the interests of museums and scholars.

Even so, many questions remain open. Who was the real owner of this treasure? Why was it buried? Perhaps the answer will never be found. What is your own guess? If you liked this story, like the video, subscribe to the channel, and tell us in the comments who you think hid this treasure.

shorts.titleEn: A Lost Hammer Led to Britain's Biggest Late Roman Treasure
shorts.text: ایک گم شدہ hammer نے Britain کی تاریخ بدل دی! یہ 16 November 1992 کی بات ہے۔ جگہ تھی Suffolk کا گاؤں Hoxne۔ کسان Peter Whatling کا hammer کھو گیا تھا۔ انہوں نے اپنے دوست Eric Lawes سے مدد مانگی۔ Eric ایک retired gardener تھے اور metal detector کا شوق رکھتے تھے۔ وہ کھیت میں detector گھمانے لگے۔ زمین سے چاندی کے چمچ نکلے، سونے کا زیور نکلا، اور بہت سے سونے چاندی کے سکے بھی۔ یہاں Eric نے ایک سمجھداری کا فیصلہ کیا۔ چند چیزیں نکالنے کے بعد انہوں نے مزید کھدائی نہیں کی۔ انہوں نے زمین کے مالکان، یعنی Suffolk County Council، اور police کو بتا دیا۔ اس کھیت کے نیچے 14,865 سکے اور تقریباً 200 چیزیں چھپی تھیں۔ لیکن اگلے دن کیا ہوا؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Aik gum shuda hammer ne Britain ki tareekh badal di! Yeh 16 November 1992 ki baat hai. Jagah thi Suffolk ka gaon Hoxne. Kisan Peter Whatling ka hammer kho gaya tha. Unhon ne apne dost Eric Lawes se madad mangi. Eric aik retired gardener thay aur metal detector ka shauq rakhte thay. Woh khet mein detector ghumane lage. Zameen se chandi ke chamach nikle, sone ka zewar nikla, aur bohat se sone chandi ke sikke bhi. Yahan Eric ne aik samajhdari ka faisla kiya. Chand cheezein nikalne ke baad unhon ne mazeed khudai nahin ki. Unhon ne zameen ke malikan, yaani Suffolk County Council, aur police ko bata diya. Is khet ke neeche 14,865 sikke aur taqriban 200 cheezein chhupi thin. Lekin agle din kya hua? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn:
A farmer lost a hammer, and a metal detectorist uncovered the largest hoard of late Roman silver and gold found in Britain.
This is how the Hoxne Hoard was discovered in 1992.

shorts.text: اخبار نے کہا £10 million! مگر کیا یہ سچ تھا؟ دوستو، Hoxne Hoard کی خبر press میں لیک ہو چکی تھی۔ 19 November 1992 کو اخبار Sun نے front page پر کہانی چھاپی۔ ساتھ میں Eric Lawes کی تصویر تھی، جس میں وہ اپنا metal detector پکڑے کھڑے تھے۔ مگر اس وقت کسی کو hoard کی پوری contents اور اصل قیمت معلوم ہی نہیں تھی۔ اس اچانک publicity کے جواب میں British Museum نے 20 November کو press conference بلائی اور دریافت کا اعلان کیا۔ پھر ایک دلچسپ بات ہوئی۔ Newspapers کی دلچسپی بہت جلد ختم ہو گئی۔ اس لیے curators نے hoard کو سکون سے sort اور clean کیا۔ ابتدائی صفائی ایک مہینے کے اندر مکمل ہو گئی۔ تو پھر اصل قیمت کتنی لگی؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Akhbar ne kaha £10 million! Magar kya yeh sach tha? Dosto, Hoxne Hoard ki khabar press mein leak ho chuki thi. 19 November 1992 ko akhbar Sun ne front page par kahani chhapi. Sath mein Eric Lawes ki tasveer thi, jis mein woh apna metal detector pakre khare thay. Magar us waqt kisi ko hoard ki poori contents aur asal qeemat maloom hi nahin thi. Is achanak publicity ke jawab mein British Museum ne 20 November ko press conference bulai aur daryaft ka elan kiya. Phir aik dilchasp baat hui. Newspapers ki dilchaspi bohat jald khatam ho gayi. Is liye curators ne hoard ko sukoon se sort aur clean kiya. Ibtidai safai aik mahine ke andar mukammal ho gayi. To phir asal qeemat kitni lagi? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.

shorts.titleEn: The Roman Pepper Pot That Looked Like an Empress
shorts.text: کیا Roman لوگ مرچ کے لیے چاندی کا برتن بناتے تھے؟ Hoxne Hoard میں ایسے 4 pepper pots ملے۔ ان کو piperatoria کہا جاتا ہے۔ ایک کا نام Empress pepper pot پڑ گیا۔ یہ کسی امیر یا شاہی خاتون کی شکل میں بنا ہے۔ اس کے بال، زیور اور کپڑے باریکی سے بنائے گئے ہیں۔ اس کے بائیں ہاتھ میں scroll ہے۔ باقی pots Hercules اور Antaeus، ibex، اور hare اور hound کی شکل میں ہیں۔ ہر pot کی بنیاد میں mechanism ہے جو اندر کی disc گھماتا ہے۔ اس سے دو سوراخ کھلتے یا بند ہوتے ہیں۔ پھر مصالحہ بھرا یا چھڑکا جا سکتا تھا۔ اسی hoard میں ایک silver tigress بھی تھی۔ اس کی شکل میں کچھ گڑبڑ تھی، کیا؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Kya Roman log mirch ke liye chandi ka bartan banate thay? Hoxne Hoard mein aise 4 pepper pots mile. In ko piperatoria kaha jata hai. Aik ka naam Empress pepper pot par gaya. Yeh kisi ameer ya shahi khatoon ki shakl mein bana hai. Is ke baal, zewar aur kapre bareeki se banaye gaye hain. Is ke bayen hath mein scroll hai. Baqi pots Hercules aur Antaeus, ibex, aur hare aur hound ki shakl mein hain. Har pot ki bunyad mein mechanism hai jo andar ki disc ghumata hai. Is se do suraakh khulte ya band hote hain. Phir masala bhara ya chhirka ja sakta tha. Isi hoard mein aik silver tigress bhi thi. Is ki shakl mein kuch garbar thi, kya? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.

The Hoxne Hoard held four silver pepper pots, including the famous Empress pepper pot.
Each had a clever rotating mechanism in its base.
